newsitem.title: FRANCE: German budget plans leave French markets unmoved.
newsitem.headline: German budget plans leave French markets unmoved.

text.p: There was virtually no reaction in Paris markets to the announcement the 1997 German budget deficit will be three percent of gross domestic product because hardly anyone believes the politicians, traders and analysts said on Friday.

Analysts said they were sceptical about the figures because the German budget deficit, which appeared previously to be heading for an overshoot, has improved miraculously without new measures being taken.

They said in any case even if the German public deficit were to overshoot a strict reading of the Maastricht treaty public deficit criterion, few were willing to bet against monetary union taking place on time.

"First of all no-one believes it, therefore it's a meaningless exercise in political showmanship. Second no matter what happens people are convinced monetary union will take place so this is merely noise on the way to an event," Stuart Thomson, chief market economist at Credit Agricole Indosuez, said.
"People are just waiting for the time when Germany says it won't hit three percent after all," he said.

Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN Amro Finance in Paris, also said he was sceptical about the apparent sudden improvement in German public finances and said investors both expected the deficit to overshoot and expected politicians to say that it wouldn't.
"They'll always keep three percent as a political target and the markets just accept they will overshoot," Brossard said. "It's too confusing to trade on."

"I'm sceptical because all the numbers we had in May and June suggested the overshoot might by enormous and now, miraculously, it's all settled without a severe tax increase," he said. "Maybe the problem was a bit less severe, but I still cannot see how they'll get to three percent."

A futures trader at a French bank underlined the mood of disdain in the Paris market place, admittedly affected somewhat by the prospect of a long weekend in France and the start of the main holiday season next week.
"At the end of the day it was a non-event. We're waiting for the real figures," he said.
The 10-year bond future remained slightly higher on the day but was unmoved after the German announcements.
The franc moved higher to 3.3760 per mark from a low of 3.3823. Traders said this was due to a rise in the dollar against the mark rather than the German budget.
The CAC-40 index of leading shares was little changed, trading slightly higher, helped by the stronger dollar.
